A raised guide can still be punished if it falls short of the whisper number.

facts.given: It beat the consensus by 5%, and it's selling off after hours. Why? ZQRT's consensus is $1.00 a share. The talk on the street, the whisper number, is $1.10. It reports $1.05. It missed the whisper number Beating the consensus is a bad sign The consensus was out of date Analysts cut estimates after a beat

reveal_json.lesson_line: Beat the consensus, miss the whisper, and it can still sell off.
reveal_json.simple: It came in under the $1.10 whisper, the street's unofficial number, and the market can treat that as the real bar.
reveal_json.why: It missed the whisper. The whisper is the unofficial number the street is really hoping for, and here it was $1.10. ZQRT cleared the official $1.00 but came in short of that, at $1.05. When the whisper is the real bar, a beat of the consensus can still disappoint. Then the stock sells off. It's a risk, not a sure thing. You won't find the whisper on any calendar. That's why the reaction matters so much. A stock selling off on a beat is telling you which bar the market used.

wrong.Analysts cut estimates after a beat: Nothing in the story says so. The whisper is the unofficial bar, not an estimate change.
wrong.Beating the consensus is a bad sign: A beat is good news. What hurts is a beat that falls short of what buyers hoped for.
wrong.The consensus was out of date: Nothing in the story says so. The gap is between the consensus and the whisper.

lesson_text: A miss has cost a lot more than a beat has paid. FactSet measures from two days before the report to two days after. Beats averaged +0.9%. Misses averaged -3.1%, about three times as big. And most companies beat, 78% on the 5-year average, so a beat is mostly expected. That's lopsided. You hold through a print to win a little, and you can lose a lot. It's why we only hold through a report when the trade is up 5R, with a cushion to take the hit. These are averages across many stocks. One name can do far worse, like Intel's 29% day. A beat pays a little, a miss costs a lot. Respect the report.

lesson_text: Price keeps going the way of the surprise. That's the drift. After a big beat, prices have tended to keep rising for over 60 trading days. After a miss, they've tended to keep falling. reveal_json.lesson_line: Judge a guided range by its midpoint, and know whose consensus you're using.
reveal_json.simple: The midpoint is $27.25 billion, just over one survey's $27.1 billion and just under the other's $27.3 billion.
reveal_json.why: Close. The midpoint sits right between the two. Read a range at its midpoint: $26 billion and $28.5 billion, added and split in half, is $27.25 billion. That's a hair over Refinitiv's $27.1 billion and a hair under the $27.3 billion Bloomberg cited. FactSet scores guided EPS ranges the same way, by the midpoint. Grab the top end and you'll see a beat that isn't there. Grab the bottom and you'll see a miss. Bloomberg called it in line.

wrong.A miss, the bottom end is $26B: That's the worst case. Read the range at its midpoint, $27.25 billion, and it lands right between the two surveys.
wrong.Can't say, a range isn't one number: You can. Read it at the midpoint, the way FactSet scores guided ranges. Here that's $27.25 billion.

prompt_json.q: Two numbers, one verdict
steps: Every quarter, put two numbers side by side. First, the company's own, most often in a press release filed with an 8-K.
Second, the consensus: the average of what the analysts expect.
Above it, a beat. Below, a miss. Right on it, in line.
Then work the surprise: actual minus consensus, divided by the consensus, times 100.
